items.title: How Grab Improved Mobile App Stability by Safely Handling Surge in AI-Generated Code Changes
items.summary:
The growing adoption of AI coding assistants has accelerated development and increased the volume of code changes per release, bringing more opportunities for defects and crashes, says Grab. To address these challenges, they implemented a layered defense strategy to prevent, detect, and contain crashes throughout the development and release lifecycle.

By Sergio De Simone

items.title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression
items.summary: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.

items.title: SpecCTMC: Exact Speculative Simulation of Diffusion Language Model Continuous-Time Markov Chains
items.summary: Masked diffusion language models offer parallel text generation, but independently sampling multiple tokens can disrupt their dependencies and change the output distribution. Exact continuous-time sampling avoids this approximation, yet typically requires one sequential model evaluation per token. We introduce SpecCTMC, a training-free speculative sampler that reduces this sequential bottleneck without a separate draft model. SpecCTMC proposes successive token updates using previously computed model predictions, evaluates their intermediate states in parallel, and applies an exact acceptance-and-correction procedure. We prove that SpecCTMC preserves the joint distribution of event times, generation order, and token values of the underlying continuous-time Markov chain. It therefore introduces neither time-discretization error nor additional factorization error from parallel decoding. Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-v0-Instruct-7B across five benchmarks demonstrate 1.73-4.38x fewer sequential model evaluations than direct continuous-time sampling, while preserving the reference sampling distribution. Our code is available at: https://github.com/kasakh/specctmc

items.title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
items.summary:
Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958).
  We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves.
  More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.

items.title: Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes
items.summary: Kinference is a new open source inference control plane for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM and Kubernetes, providing token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:introducing kinference an open source inference control plane for vllm and kuber
items.content_excerpt: We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference] , a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM. We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients.. In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request. Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks , we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type. By incorporating cache awareness into policies, platform owners can create policies that will send simple requests to the cheaper model — but only if that’s less work than sending them to the expensive model in the first place. In our unloaded latency benchmark above, we sought to measure the effect of Kinference’s KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation. In our capacity benchmark, below, we measured the requests per minute can each endpoint can serve within a latency SLO. In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn . items.title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.summary: Explore 3 principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows and how human-review is a strategic imperative for production-ready agents.
items.story_key: story|title:why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
items.content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. items.title: Maggie Appleton: Agentic Coding Has Outgrown the Text Box
items.summary:
Agentic coding has outgrown the text box. Maggie Appleton, staff research engineer at GitHub Next, argues that walls of CLI output and AGENTS.md files serve coding agents far better than the humans steering them. She walks through Chopin, the GitHub Next prototype where background agents turn a team's planning chat into a structured plan, and makes the case for agents that prompt you instead of waiting to be prompted.

What we cover:
– Why text-heavy agentic coding tools favor agents over humans
– Boundary objects: what AGENTS.md, skill files and MCP servers get right and wrong
– Multiplayer planning with coding agents in GitHub Next's Chopin
– Human-to-agent handoffs, formal verification and spec-driven development
– Why software quality is rising, not falling, with coding agents
– Which roles still matter: PMs, designers and engineers

items.title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
items.summary: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.

items.title: Multimodal-SEA: Benchmarking AI Agent Security under Multimodal Social Engineering Attacks
items.summary: Personal AI agents face social engineering attacks supported by forged multimodal content, but existing evaluations mainly focus on text-based dialogue, leaving their intrinsic security under such attacks insufficiently studied. We introduce Multimodal-SEA, an interactive benchmark comprising 608 expert-designed tasks grounded in real-world fraud cases, covering 14 domains and 152 attack scenarios with prepared multimodal content. The tasks span four difficulty levels and reflect the distinct social and cultural contexts of Chinese and English environments. Agents inspect content, verify requests, and execute actions in simulated applications, with attack outcomes grounded in verifiable tool execution logs. To enable controlled red teaming of personal agents, we design a multimodal attack harness that integrates task information, attack progression control, and multimodal content construction to evaluate their intrinsic security against adaptive social engineering attacks in simulated environments. Evaluating seven widely used multimodal models across six dimensions reveals that all are vulnerable, with attack success rates of 7.1% to 34.5%. Adding multimodal content increases attack success from 19.9% to 29.2%, despite increased proactive verification coverage. Stronger safety instructions reduce attack success without improving recognition of deceptive multimodal content, while lower attack success rates for some models accompany excessive refusal of legitimate requests.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.317
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
  • Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
  • Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
  • Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do
  • Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view
  • Added anthropic.plan, anthropic.seat_type, anthropic.provider and anthropic.custom_base_url to OTel metrics, events and spans
  • Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group
  • Added a daily record of each developer's IdP groups on Claude apps gateways with admin: set, kept for admin.identity_retention_days, which the cost report groups by
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NESTED_SESSION_ID: set it to 1 on a self-hosted runner to have claude -p run inside a session use that session's ID and transcript, as in earlier versions
  • Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn when an LLM gateway set as the base URL answers 403 or 422 to its server-side safety check (a 403 with an apiKeyHelper is unchanged)
  • Fixed claude auth status exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed a project's effortLevel setting being ignored by sessions that an app starts ahead of time and then opens in the project, such as new sessions in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed claude --from-pr reporting "No conversations found" in projects with many sessions when the linked session was older than the first page
  • Fixed the second of two simultaneous permission prompts showing no file path or command on claude.ai and the mobile apps
  • Fixed Remote Control and SDK hosts offering "don't ask again" on a mod's tool calls
  • Fixed session titles being lost in cloud and SDK sessions when a new message or Stop arrived while the title was generating
  • Fixed self-paced /loop wakeups sometimes not being scheduled when Claude left a field out of its request
  • Fixed auto mode in cloud sessions stopping for approval when the Artifact tool uploaded, wrote to a database or saved a file through the outputs folder
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai being lost or downloaded again every ten minutes when they can't be written to disk
  • Fixed /schedule leaving a cloud scheduled task's next run time and link out of its results after creating or updating it
  • Fixed screen readers speaking a running subagent's elapsed time and token count on every change in screen reader mode
  • Fixed a region or network block (HTTP 403) being shown as a sign-in failure; the error now explains the block
  • Fixed Claude saying a working claude.ai connector needed authorization or had failed in cloud sessions when a synced plugin included the same server
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 when a full disk or quota lost its transcript or ~/.claude.json writes; it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1. Full NFS exports may be missed
  • Fixed edits to settings files made in the first second or so after launch not taking effect until a settings file changed again
  • Fixed old transcripts not being cleaned up on machines where some runs skip cleanup, such as runs using --setting-sources
  • Fixed deleted agent team inboxes being re-created by a teammate's late message
  • Fixed a re-created agent teammate being removed from its team by an earlier shutdown approval
  • Fixed stored scheduled tasks being impossible to list or delete after scheduled tasks were turned off
  • Fixed Claude deleting your most recently updated /team-onboarding guide when asked to delete one without naming which
  • Fixed Claude saying a /team-onboarding guide was deleted when the server refused the delete
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway hiding Amazon Bedrock's "Input is too long." error, which left sessions failing every turn with "upstream rejected the request" instead of compacting
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions losing recent turns or the whole conversation when restarted while a plan waited for approval
  • Fixed "Prompt is too long" after automatic compaction in sessions whose very large CLAUDE.md changed since it was last sent
  • Fixed high memory use and slow startup in headless sessions with many plugins that register commands
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers receiving an empty AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK when their env config sets it to empty; the variable is now unset, so the server can use the machine's own AWS credentials
  • Fixed API requests failing with "unable to get local issuer certificate" behind some TLS-inspecting proxies after a root certificate renewal
  • Fixed very long conversations losing their earlier summary when compaction had to shorten its own request
  • Fixed a PDF's own metadata being able to make Read and @-mentions under-count its pages
  • Fixed DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_OPUS and DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_SONNET having no effect on [1m], other-region and undated spellings of the default model
  • Fixed /artifacts and the Artifact tool's shared list showing no shared artifacts when you have 200 or more of your own
  • Fixed Claude treating partial Grep and Glob results as complete when a search hit its time limit
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports to an https:// endpoint through a proxy never being sent when they started while another export was still in progress
  • Fixed a flood of connection attempts to a proxy that blocks (HTTP 403) OpenTelemetry exports to an http:// endpoint
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports hanging indefinitely behind a proxy that never answers; they now time out after 10 seconds, or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT up to 30 seconds
  • Fixed resumed sessions telling Claude again about a file change it already knew about
  • Fixed Claude sometimes not using a built-in tool in a resumed session after an earlier call failed because the tool was switched off
  • Fixed /remote-control answering "Unknown command" instead of saying that Remote Control is turned off by the disableRemoteControl setting
  • Fixed agent team teammates in tmux or iTerm2 panes starting in auto mode when the lead session was in manual mode
  • Fixed a background session sometimes losing a just-made change of permission mode when it was upgraded or retired
  • Fixed Ctrl+C stopping all running background agents when pressed to clear typed text at the prompt
  • Fixed /feedback showing "Enter to confirm" while a report is being sent
  • Fixed child processes of a stopped shell command sometimes being sent SIGTERM twice, which could make some programs skip their cleanup
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session sharing that session's ID: it wrote into the session's transcript, and a restart could resume the wrong conversation
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session generating a title of its own and sending it to that session
  • Improved the error shown on Microsoft Foundry when Azure credentials can't be loaded: it now says to check or refresh them, and reports as cloud_credential_error
  • Improved /design-sync to say up front when your design system has moved to Claude, and stop before building instead of failing at upload
  • Improved the startup error when a required Claude apps gateway can't be reached: it points to the network instead of a sign-in, and says when the gateway's TLS certificate can't be verified
  • Improved the "Resume this session with" hint shown at exit to repeat the flags you launched with (for example --chrome --debug) ahead of --resume
  • Improved how self-hosted runners recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a runner's next poll now opens a new connection instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a session now opens new connections instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover when connections stop answering: after a heartbeat gets no answer, a session now opens new connections instead of trying each idle one in turn
  • Changed SendMessage so a message to a running background agent arrives earlier: its running command moves to the background, without being stopped
  • Changed subagents and teammates on a different model from the main conversation to use that model's saved effort level or its default, instead of the session's effort level
  • Changed exit to skip the "Background work is running" prompt for plugin monitors
  • Changed the built-in plugin-authoring skill to offer once, after a mod you built works, to help share the mod
  • Removed the Read tool's "file unchanged since your last Read" stub: reading an unchanged file again returns its content
  • Windows: Fixed every tool call being refused on some volumes where the native path lookup fails; the working-directory check now compares the folder's identity instead
  • Windows: Fixed the session scratchpad and other temporary paths growing with your project's path length in sessions not started by Claude Desktop, which made repositories cloned into them hit the 260-character path limit
  • Gateway: Fixed the status line and /usage showing a developer's own spend limit as 100% used after their group's pooled budget ran out
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed Claude not seeing the interrupted tool call when a session moves to a new runner and the turn is older than CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN_MAX_AGE_MS
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server that was switched off coming back on after the session moved to a new machine, when the session service had refused to save the switch
  • Remote Control: Improved fork names when the app doesn't set one: a long name keeps its "(fork)" ending, and in sessions started with claude remote-control a fork of "Name (fork)" is "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed forked conversations dropping messages: only one of the tool calls Claude ran in parallel was kept, and the last messages a compaction kept were lost, which could leave Claude's answer without the question it answered
  • [VSCode] Fixed a message being lost when Claude did not finish starting in time: the extension now starts Claude once more before showing the error
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen opening when a request is blocked for its region or network
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Account panel showing the plan name with a lower-cased second word
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening on top of the chat instead of in another editor group
  • [VSCode] Fixed attachment chips, menus, banners and dialogs in the Claude panel staying small when chat.fontSize is raised
  • [VSCode] Fixed ultrathink not raising effort for its turn or showing its rainbow when telemetry is off
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a link card to cloud sessions, so you can open or decline a link an MCP server asks you to visit instead of the request going unseen
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the organization environment dialog in admin settings to the personal dialogs' short layout: each section opens from a row, and unsaved input asks before closing
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed adding a network secret for a host that already has one silently replacing it; the Add secret form now refuses and points you to the existing secret
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed new scheduled tasks ignoring your organization's default environment: the form now starts on the one an admin chose instead of the Anthropic-hosted default
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the next message to an idle session going unanswered after you restart claude remote-control, when you sent it within a minute of your previous message
  • [Claude Tag] Changed newly pasted artifact links in Slack to show a simpler card with an Open button that opens the artifact in Claude, instead of Slack's side panel
release_highlights: Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
